Antler score (typical)

Measure in inches with a flexible steel tape, along the outer curve. Tines (G1, G2…) from the top of the main beam to the tip. Circumferences: H1 at the smallest place between the burr and G1, then between each pair of tines.

Chronic wasting disease (CWD): if you hunt in another state, many states, including New York, don't allow whole carcasses back in. Bring deboned meat, cleaned skull caps and hides, and check the rules where you hunt. Don't eat meat from a deer that acted sick.

Rough averages: field-dressed deer weigh about 78% of live weight and give about 40–50% of dressed weight as boneless meat, less with a lot of shot damage.

Arrow speed

No chronograph needed. Lay the phone next to you, shoot at a target at a measured distance, and the phone times the gap between the shot and the hit. From that it works out your arrow speed, then your energy, momentum and how far a deer can drop ("jump the string") before the arrow gets there.

Measure the distance with a rangefinder; a 1-yard error changes the speed by about 5% at 20 yards. Temperature matters a little because sound travels faster in warm air.

2 · Measure

Tap Start listening, then shoot. Keep the phone within a couple of feet of the bow (or of the target), and keep talking and other noise down. A target that makes a solid "thwack" (a bag or foam block) works best.

3 · String jump

Sound travels about 4 times faster than an arrow. A deer hears the bow, reacts, and drops its body to spring away before the arrow arrives. How far it can drop depends on your arrow speed, the distance, and how alert the deer is.

    Tapping the map
    • Walk each square slowly in lanes a few yards apart. Look low (leaves, grass stems) and at knee height (brush the deer rubbed past).
    • Squares turn gray as you walk through them with GPS on; tap a square to mark or unmark it.

    • Hit deer often go downhill, toward water and thick cover, and may circle back. Check the edges of thickets and creek banks.

    Route in and out

    AI hunt spots

    Finds the places where deer are most likely to move or bed within about 1 km, from the shape of the land, satellite land cover (food, water, cover), today's wind and the rut.
    NFunnelSSaddleFFood (field edge)BBenchPRidge pointWWaterCThick coverYYoung growthDDrawAHardwoods (acorns?)ZBeddingStand spot (downwind)

    How it works: a model on your phone reads the elevation data the way an experienced hunter reads a topo map, and the yearly satellite land-cover map (Annual NLCD, from Landsat, 30 m detail) for fields, crops, young growth, thick cover and water. Then it adds today's wind (set in Wind & weather), thermals, the rut phase and nearby houses. It can't see deer, this year's crops or acorns, so treat the spots as places to scout first.

    Deer movement

    A forecast of when deer are most likely on their feet, built from what research shows matters most: time of day, time of year (the rut) and weather. It's a guide for planning your sits, not a guarantee.

    Location
    Weather can't be loaded inside Claude, so this shows the forecast from time of day and the rut only. On the website version the forecast also uses the weather for the next 16 days.
    Today—
    Best times—
    Why this score

    Next days

    Tap a day to see its hours and reasons. Forecast weather is good for about 3 days, fair to 7, rough after that.

    Rut in New York and New Jersey

    Pre-rut Oct 15–31 · Seeking Nov 1–7 · Chasing Nov 8–14 · Peak breeding Nov 15–22 · Post-rut Nov 23–Dec 5 · Second rut Dec 6–20
    Peak breeding in the Northeast is mid-November (state fetal and fawning data put it around Nov 11–20). Dates shift a few days with the deer herd and the year.
    What the research says
    • Time of day matters most. GPS-collared deer move mostly around sunrise and sunset. The best hours are usually the first two after first light and the last two before dark.
    • Time of year is next. Bucks moved about 20% more during the rut than after it, and they move in daylight most during seeking and chasing in early to mid November.
    • Colder than normal helps. Temperature was the only weather factor with a consistent effect: in fall and winter deer moved more on colder days. Unusually warm days slow daytime movement.
    • Strong wind and rain slow deer down. Movement drops as wind gets stronger, and deer move little during steady rain; they often move right after it stops.
    • Pressure and moon: little proof. Collar studies found no consistent effect of barometric pressure or moon phase, so the app gives them almost no weight. A cold front counts mainly for the cooler air behind it.
    • Hunting pressure. Heavy pressure, such as opening weekend of firearms season on public land, pushes deer to move more at night and in thick cover. Hunt escape routes and thick cover then.

    Based on GPS-collar research (Webb et al. 2010), a Pennsylvania trail-camera study, and state rut data. Your own trail cameras and scouting beat any forecast.

    Scouting & sign

    Read sign like a pro, log what you find, and learn where the pressure really is.

    How old is this sign?

    Rain and snow at your spot (from the weather record) put a clock on tracks and scrapes.
    Checking the last rain and snow…
    Tracks
    • Fresh: sharp, crisp edges, dewclaw marks clean, no leaves or debris inside, dirt darker and damp where it was pushed up.
    • Older: edges crumbled or rounded, debris or bug tracks inside, dirt dried to the same color as around it.
    • After rain: raindrop pits inside the track mean it was made before the rain; a crisp track over smooth, rain-packed dirt was made after it.
    • In snow: no new snow inside = made after the last snowfall. Melted, rounded or crusted edges = a day or more old; a frozen crust inside often means it was made before a cold night.
    Rubs
    • Fresh: bright, light-colored wood that still looks wet, bark shavings lying on the ground or on top of the leaves, sap still sticky.
    • Older: wood turned gray or brown, edges of bark dried and curled, shavings faded or covered.
    • Big rubs on big trees, rubbed again year after year, are a buck's signpost: log every visit.
    Scrapes
    • Active: bare, damp dirt pawed clean of leaves, often with a track in it, a strong musky smell, and the licking branch above broken, chewed or bent.
    • Old: leaves blown back in, dirt dry and crusted, no smell.
    • Clear the leaves out of a scrape when you find it; if it is clean again on your next visit, a buck worked it since.
    Droppings
    • Fresh (hours): shiny, wet-looking, dark, soft enough to squash.
    • A day or two: dull outside, still moist inside.
    • Old: dry, crumbly, lighter in color. Pellets in fall and winter; soft clumps mean lush, green food.
    Beds
    • Fresh: oval of pressed-down leaves or grass, still flat, sometimes warm; in snow, melted down to the leaves, hair in the bed.
    • Older: leaves fluffing back up, frost or new snow in it.
    • Big single beds on points and benches, facing downhill with the wind at the back, are often bucks.

    Mast report: which oaks are dropping

    From your white oak, red oak and fruit tree pins. On the map, tap the pin, Log a visit, and count acorns on the ground in a 1-yard circle under it. White oaks drop first and deer hit them first.

    Pressure log

    One tap at the lot or in the woods. Uses your GPS. After a few weeks you'll see when and where other hunters really go.
    See it on the map (Layers: Pressure you logged)

    New piece of public land?

    Plan one efficient scouting loop through saddles, benches, funnels, food and water, walked with the wind in your face. Then use Approach on the map to check your walk-in against bedding.
    Plan a scouting loop

    Public-land stand rules

    • New York state land (6 NYCRR 190.8): label the stand with your name and address or license number; place and use it only during big game, turkey or migratory bird season; nothing that injures the tree: no nails, screws, screw-in steps or permanent stands.
    • New Jersey state parks and forests: label with your Conservation ID (CID) and contact info; up no more than 30 days before the season, down within 14 days after; one stand or blind at a time; nothing that pierces a tree; no dead or diseased trees.
    • New Jersey WMAs: rules differ; check the NJ Hunting Digest for that WMA.
    • Each stand pin shows these rules, and you can set a Remove stand by date in the pin.
    Rules change. Confirm with NY DEC or NJ Fish & Wildlife before the season.

    Better GPS in the timber

    • Dual-frequency GPS phones (many newer Android phones, e.g. recent Pixel and Galaxy models) hold much better under hemlock and in hollows.
    • A Bluetooth GPS receiver (Garmin GLO 2, Bad Elf type) clipped high on your pack is the biggest upgrade. On Android, pair it and set it as the location source with a mock-location app; this app then uses it automatically.
    • Phone in an outer chest pocket or held up, not deep in a pack. Cold drains batteries and slows GPS: keep it warm.
    • Under thick cover, turn on Pace mode in navigation so your steps keep moving you on the map.
    • Save pins in openings when you can, and use Refine here on later visits.

    If you are lost or hurt

    • Stop and stay put if you are hurt or truly lost: searchers find people who stay in one place.
    • Call 911 and read them the coordinates above. A text may go through when a call won't.
    • Three blasts on a whistle (or three shots where legal) is the signal for help. Wear your blaze orange.
    • Save battery: dim the screen, close other apps, turn on battery saver. Keep the phone warm in an inside pocket.
    • Tree-stand fall: don't move someone with a possible neck or back injury unless they are in danger.
    • Before every hunt, use the check-in timer so someone knows when to expect you.

    Deer tracking

    Everything for after the shot, in order: what you hit, when to go, and the tools to find your deer.

    1 · Right after the shot

    • Watch the deer as far as you can and listen: a crash, a cough, running water, then quiet.
    • Note the last spot you saw it (a tree, a rock) and where it stood when you shot.
    • Stay put. Tap Start: I just shot, pick where it hit, and check your arrow.
    Shot timer · when to track · can I hang it overnight?
    Where did the arrow hit?
    How to tell where you hit

    2 · Tracking tools

    Blood pins and search gridPin the hit site and every drop on the map. Lost blood? The grid shows where to search. Blood trail cameraMakes blood stand out on brown leaves and dirt. Track finderBrings out faint hoofprints in mud, dirt and snow. Map and navigationPin the shot spot and last-seen spot, then walk back to them exactly.

    3 · Tracking kit

    Keep these in your pack all season. Tick them off as you pack; the app remembers.

    4 · Tracking tips

    • Mark first, then follow. Pin the shot spot and the first blood before you move on, and drop an LED marker light at each blood spot. If you lose the trail, go back to the last light.
    • Go slow and quiet, one person on the blood, one looking ahead. Look at knee height on brush and on both sides of the trail.
    • Blood dries and darkens fast. Dried blood looks brown or black; wet blood shines in a flashlight.
    • Trail ran out? Start a search grid from the last blood. Check the nearest water, thick cover and downhill first: hurt deer often go there.
    • If you jump a bedded deer, stop. Back out quietly and give it more time.
    • At night, a bright white light shows blood best. Carry a spare battery and mark your truck on the map.
    • Tracking dogs: a leashed blood-tracking dog can find deer people can't. New York licenses leashed tracking-dog handlers; check your state's rules. United Blood Trackers lists volunteer dog handlers.
    United Blood Trackers

    Blood trail

    Point the camera at the ground along the trail. Possible blood is shown bright red and ringed; everything else turns gray, so drops on brown leaves are easier to spot.

    Pin blood spots on the map
    5
    Possible blood spots0
    Tracking tips
    • Red leaves, berries and some mushrooms look like blood to the camera too. Check every ring with your own eyes before you follow it.
    • At night use a bright white light. A red headlamp makes blood look dark and almost disappear.
    • Unsure if a spot is blood? A drop of hydrogen peroxide fizzes on blood.
    • Mark the last blood you found with flagging tape before searching ahead, so you can always go back to it.
    • Look on both sides of the trail and on brush and grass at the height of the deer's body, not only on the ground.
    • In low light hold the phone steady, or tap Capture, because a blurry frame hides small drops.

    How to blood-track a whitetail

    Most lost deer are lost in the first minutes after the shot: by moving too soon, or by not marking where the deer was hit and last seen. Follow these steps in order.

    1. Stay put and watch. Note how the deer reacted: a mule kick or hard run with a low head often means a heart or lung hit; a hunched, slow walk with the tail clamped often means a gut hit. Watch and listen until it's out of sight; a crash in the distance is a good sign.
    2. Mark two spots before they fade from memory. Where the deer stood when you shot, and the last place you saw it. Pick a tree or rock for each, take a compass bearing, and drop markers in Maps (type: Blood / recovery).
    3. Read the sign at the hit site. Quietly find your arrow or the first blood, without walking the trail. Use the table below to judge the hit, then wait the right amount of time.
    4. Wait. Pushing a wounded deer is the most common way to lose it: it will bed, then run farther if jumped. If in doubt, wait longer. Back out quietly if you need to.
    5. Track slowly, with one or two people. Mark the last blood with flagging tape or toilet paper every so often so you can always go back and see the direction of travel. Look ahead and on both sides, on leaves, grass and brush at the deer's body height, not just on the ground. Track marks and kicked-up leaves count too. Use Track in Maps to record your path.
    6. If the blood stops, go back to the last blood. Search in widening circles or a grid from there. Check thick cover, low ground, creek bottoms and water, and old trails leading away. Don't trample the last sign.
    7. If you jump the deer, stop. Note where it bedded, back out quietly, and give it several more hours.
    8. Approach a downed deer from behind, from the back and above if you can. Eyes open and glazed usually means it's dead; touch the eye with a long stick from behind to be sure. Be ready for a legal follow-up shot if needed.
    9. Tag it right away and report the harvest as your state requires before you move it far.
    Read the sign: blood, hair and wait times
    Heart / both lungsBright red blood, often pink and frothy with bubbles; heavy, sprayed blood; deer usually runs hard and crashes within 100 yd
    Bow: 30–60 minGun: 30 min
    One lung / high lungBright red, some bubbles, blood may start light then increase
    Bow: 2–3 hoursGun: 1–2 hours
    LiverDark red, rich blood; steady drops; deer often walks off and beds within a few hundred yards
    Bow: 3–4 hoursGun: 2–3 hours
    Gut / paunchDark or watery blood mixed with green or brown matter, strong stomach smell, little blood; deer hunched
    Bow: 8–12 hours, overnight if coolGun: 6–8 hours
    Muscle / leg / brisketBright red, no bubbles, heavy at first then thinning; long white or coarse hair
    Bow: 2–4 hours, then track; often survivesGun: 1–2 hours
    Not sureLittle blood, mixed sign
    Bow: At least 3 hoursGun: At least 1–2 hours
    • Hair color tells you where: long white hair often means a low hit (belly or brisket); dark brown, coarse hair means the back or upper side; short gray-brown hair is typical of the chest.
    • Warm weather or rain coming? Meat can spoil and rain washes blood away. You may need to start sooner on a likely-fatal hit, but go slowly and be ready to back out if the deer is still alive.
    • Is it blood? A drop of hydrogen peroxide fizzes and foams on blood. Use the camera view above to make blood stand out on red and brown leaves.
    Tracking at night
    • Use a bright white light. Blood is hardest to see under red and green light, and some hunters find a warm-white or blood-tracking light helps.
    • Rules on carrying a bow or gun while tracking after legal hours differ; if you're unsure, leave it behind or call your state's conservation police first.
    • Tell someone where you are, bring a spare light, and record your path with Track in Maps so you can get back out.
    Call a tracking dog

    A trained, leashed tracking dog finds many deer that people can't, even the next day. New York requires the handler to hold a DEC leashed tracking dog license, and the handler must notify an Environmental Conservation Officer before tracking. New Jersey requires a Certified Deer Tracking Dog Permit. Call a licensed handler before you walk all over the trail, and don't track onto someone else's land without permission.

    NY DEC: leashed tracking dog licenseUnited Blood Trackers: find a tracker near you

    Wait times are common guidelines from experienced trackers, not rules; every deer and hit is different. When in doubt, wait longer.

    Track finder

    Tracks are shallow dents, so what you see is their shadows. Hold a flashlight low to the ground, almost flat, shining across the track, and point the camera straight down. The views below make those shadows stronger.

    6
    315°
    Turn "Light from" until the track pops out. It only changes the Relief view.
    Trail scan: hold the phone at chest height and pan slowly across the ground. Brighter and darker bands are boosted, and smooth, packed ground (fewer leaves and twigs than around it) is tinted yellow. Tree trunks, rocks and logs are smooth too and can be tinted. Works best with low sun, frost, wet ground or light snow. It helps your eyes; it does not detect trails by itself.

    Measure the track

    Lay a coin or other object of known size beside the track, in the same photo, and hold the phone straight above. Tap both ends of the object, then the tip and heel of the track.
    inches

    Camo check

    Take a photo of yourself (or your camo) in the woods. Tap on the camo, then tap on the background right next to it. The score shows how far apart the two look to you and to a deer.

    ΔE is the color difference between the two spots. Under about 10 they blend together, 10–25 is noticeable, over 25 stands out. Fine camo patterns also blur together for a deer, so they matter less than overall color and brightness.

    Movement

    Deer notice motion long before they make out color or shape. Point the camera at a scene and move: everything that moves glows orange, everything still fades to a dim deer-like gray.

    Movement mode needs the live camera, which works on the website version of this app, not inside Claude.

    A deer's nose is its best defense. Your scent drifts downwind in a cone, wider in light, shifting wind. Set up so the deer you expect are upwind of you.

    Test & calibrate

    1. Calibrate: figure-8. Hold the phone flat, then slowly draw a big figure 8 in the air 3 times, turning your wrist so the phone tilts every way. Step away from trucks, tree-stand steel, gun barrels and magnets in phone cases first.
    2. Steadiness test. Lay the phone flat and still (on a stump or your pack) and tap Test.
    3. Turn test. Hold the phone flat in front of you and turn slowly all the way around once (about 20 seconds). Jumps mean metal nearby or a bad calibration.
    4. Accuracy check against something you know. Pick one:

    Sun & moon

    Location

    Solunar times

    Deer movement usually peaks around dawn and dusk. Legal hunting hours are set by each state and differ between NY and NJ, so check your current hunting guide before you go.

    Shine finder

    Reflections from a watch, glasses, a scope lens, a phone screen or a shiny gun barrel flash bright to a deer even when your colors blend in. Photograph yourself in your gear, ideally with a flash or in sun, and the app rings the shiny spots.

    5
    Shiny spots found0

    The finder looks for very bright, colorless spots. Plain white objects such as paper or a white cooler also show up, so judge each ring yourself.

    Skyline check

    A dark shape against bright sky stands out to a deer no matter what camo you wear. Take a photo from where a deer would stand, looking toward your spot. Orange lines mark outlines against the sky.

    Approximate values. A deer's eyes sit on the sides of its head, giving it about 310° of view with only about 50–60° seen by both eyes and a blind spot of about 50° straight behind. A person sees about 200°, with about 120° seen by both eyes.

    Hunter's guide

    Regular detergents often contain UV (optical) brighteners. They make fabric glow in ultraviolet light, which deer can likely see. The guides below list detergents labeled free of them and show how to check your own gear.

    Good detergents (no UV brighteners)
    Scent Killer Gold Laundry Detergent
    Wildlife Research Center · hunting · label claim
    Dead Down Wind Laundry Detergent
    Dead Down Wind · hunting · label claim
    Sport-Wash
    Atsko · hunting and outdoor · label claim
    Scent-A-Way Laundry Detergent
    Hunter's Specialties · hunting · label claim

    ElimiShield · hunting · label claim
    Phaze Laundry Detergent
    Illusion Hunting Systems · hunting · label claim
    Free & Clear Liquid Laundry Detergent
    Seventh Generation · grocery store, unscented · label claim
    • Pick the unscented (odorless) version where there is a choice. Some hunting detergents also come in earth or pine scents.
    • Skip fabric softener and dryer sheets; they add scent.
    • Run the washer empty once first, because leftover regular detergent can put brighteners back on your gear.
    • Clothes already washed with brighteners can stay bright for a long time. Check them with a UV flashlight in a dark room; a UV-blocking spray such as Atsko U-V Killer is sold for treating them.
    • Formulas change, so check the bottle says "no UV brighteners" when you buy it.
    How to check your clothes for UV brighteners
    Safety warning. UV light can damage your eyes and skin. Never look into the beam and never shine it at anyone's eyes, including your own, children's or pets'. Watch for reflections off mirrors, glass and shiny surfaces. Don't shine it on your skin, and keep your hands out of the beam while you check. Wear UV-blocking glasses (labeled UV400) if you use the light often, and keep it away from children.
    1. Use a flashlight sold as 365 nm. Cheaper 395 nm lights also give off a lot of visible violet light, which makes the glow hard to judge.
    2. Go into a fully dark room and give your eyes a minute or two to adjust.
    3. Test the light first on a sheet of white printer paper. Most printer paper contains brighteners and glows bright blue-white, so you know what a "positive" looks like.
    4. Hold the light about 30–50 cm (1–1.5 ft) from the fabric and sweep slowly over every piece: jacket, pants, base layers, hat, gloves, face mask, backpack and boots.
    5. Look closely at seams, stitching, labels, logos and zipper tapes. Thread and tags often glow even when the fabric doesn't.
    6. Anything that glows blue-white has brighteners. Rewash it a few times in one of the Good detergents, or treat it with a UV-blocking spray, then check again.
    7. Check before each season, and again after anything is washed in a regular machine or with someone else's laundry.
    How deer see: what this app simulates
    • Two color cones instead of three. Deer cones peak near 455 nm (blue) and 537 nm (green). With no red-sensitive cone, reds and oranges lose their color and fall toward dull olive or gray. Blaze orange is bright to you and to other hunters, but not to deer.
    • Lower sharpness. Acuity is estimated at roughly 20/100, sharpest along a horizontal band at eye level (the visual streak) and blurrier above and below it. Set the horizon slider to where the skyline or the deer's eye level falls in your photo.
    • Light conditions. The Light menu puts the same light on both halves so you can compare. In dim light both you and the deer lose color and sharpness, but the deer side stays much brighter: deer eyes are packed with rods and have a reflective layer (tapetum) behind the retina. Fog adds a haze that is thickest near the horizon line. Start from a daytime photo; the brightness levels are an illustration of the trend, not measurements.
    • Headlamp. The beam lights a spot in the middle of the frame. Try it with Dark night or Full moon night. White and green light look bright to a deer, because green is close to the peak of its color cone and its night vision. Red light looks much dimmer to a deer than to you, because deer have no red-sensitive cone. UV light is nearly invisible to you, but a deer's eye lets UV through, so it likely sees the glow. Brighteners in your clothes would also light up under UV, which a camera photo can't show.

    Limits. Phone cameras filter out ultraviolet, so the app can't show UV brighteners in washed clothing, which can glow to deer. It also can't show a deer's nearly 300° field of view or how strongly deer react to movement. The blur is calculated for a typical phone lens; use Zoom 3× to judge it, since a small screen hides fine detail anyway.
